intro.html: Reading passages love arguments: a scientist defends a theory, a critic attacks a book, two historians disagree. To follow them you need words that rate an argument, from rock-solid to falling apart.

Strong: cogent (clear and convincing), trenchant (sharp and to the point), valid (logically sound), and three that mean no one can knock it down: irrefutable, incontrovertible, unassailable. Weak: tenuous (thin, slight), flimsy (easily broken), untenable (impossible to defend). And moot: open to debate, or no longer worth debating.
Look inside the long ones. Irrefutable is not able to be refuted; incontrovertible is not able to be turned against (contra + vert); untenable is not able to be held (ten, hold).

words.ex: Rosa made a {cogent} case for a longer lunch break, complete with charts.
words.ctx: The lawyer’s argument was {cogent}: each point followed clearly from the last, and by the end even the doubtful jurors were nodding.
words.etym: From Latin cogens, “compelling,” from cogere (to drive together): co- (together) + agere (to drive).

mn.text: In Ada’s argument every point fits the next like the cogs of a clock, so the whole thing turns smoothly: it is {cogent}.

scene.alt: A scientist points proudly at three gears that fit together perfectly.

words.def: sharp, clear and forceful, cutting straight to the point
words.ex: The coach’s {trenchant} comments at halftime showed the team exactly what was going wrong.
words.ctx: Unlike the other reviewers, who praised the film vaguely, Ms. Lin wrote a {trenchant} critique that named its three biggest flaws in plain, sharp words.
words.etym: From Old French trenchant, “cutting,” from trenchier (to cut), the same source as trench.

mn.cue: the TRENCH COAT detective: sharp and clear
mn.text: The detective in the trench coat sums up the case in one sharp, clear line: “The cake thief has frosting on his sleeve.” Her remark is {trenchant}.

scene.alt: A detective in a trench coat points her magnifying glass at a startled cake thief.

words.def: logically correct or well grounded; also, officially accepted
words.ex: Your library card is {valid} for one more year.
words.ctx: The argument is {valid}, since its conclusion follows from its premises, but it is still wrong, because one of those premises is false.
words.etym: From Latin validus, “strong,” from valere (to be strong).

mn.cue: VAL + ID: Val’s ID is accepted
mn.text: At the gate, Val shows her ID; it is real and up to date, so the guard waves her through. Her ID is {valid}.

scene.alt: A woman named Val shows her ID at a station gate, and the guard waves her through.

words.ex: The video replay was {irrefutable} proof that the ball crossed the line.
words.ctx: Scientists once doubted that the continents move, but measurements from satellites now offer {irrefutable} evidence that they drift a few centimeters every year.
words.etym: From in- (not) + refutable, from Latin refutare (to push back, prove wrong).

mn.text: Pip says he didn’t eat the cookies, but crumbs cover his face and his hand is still in the jar: the proof is {irrefutable}.

scene.alt: A boy with cookie crumbs all over his face insists it was not him, while his mother points.

words.def: so certain that no one can dispute it
words.ex: The photo finish was {incontrovertible}: the blue runner won by an inch.
words.ctx: Historians had argued for years about when the old bridge was built, but the builder’s signed and dated plans, found in an attic, were {incontrovertible}.
words.etym: From in- (not) + controvertible, from Latin controversus (turned against, disputed): contra (against) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: Sven and Tia argue over whose watermelon is heavier until the scale settles it: no controversy now. The answer is {incontrovertible}.

scene.alt: Two farmers stop arguing when a scale shows which watermelon is heavier.

words.def: too strong to be attacked or questioned
words.ex: With a twenty-point lead and two minutes left, the team’s position looked {unassailable}.
words.ctx: Her reputation for honesty was {unassailable}; in forty years of running the store, she had never once shortchanged a customer.
words.etym: From un- (not) + assailable, from assail (to attack), from Latin ad- (at) + salire (to leap).

mn.cue: un-a-SAIL-able: no ship can SAIL in
mn.text: The pirates sail at the island fort again and again, but its walls never give way: the fort is {unassailable}.

scene.alt: A pirate ship turns back from a strong fort high on a rocky island.

words.ex: The kitten kept a {tenuous} grip on the top of the curtain.
words.ctx: The link between the two thefts was {tenuous}, resting only on the fact that both happened on a Tuesday, so the detective kept looking for stronger evidence.

mn.text: The tent is held up by one thin, wobbly pole, and the next breeze could knock it down: its hold is {tenuous}.

scene.alt: A boy watches nervously as his tent leans in the wind, barely standing.

words.def: weak and easily broken; also, hard to believe
words.ex: The {flimsy} umbrella turned inside out at the first gust of wind.
words.ctx: His excuse was {flimsy}: he said he missed practice because his shoelaces were untied, and no one believed him for a second.

mn.text: Kai’s kite is made of film-thin paper and two twigs, and the first gust rips it in half: it is {flimsy}.

scene.alt: A boy watches his thin paper kite tear apart in the wind.

words.def: impossible to defend, keep or hold on to
words.ex: With the river rising around the campsite, staying another night was {untenable}.
words.ctx: Once an older map turned up, the claim that the village was founded in 1850 became {untenable}, because the map, dated 1820, already showed the village.
words.etym: From un- (not) + tenable, from French tenir (to hold), from Latin tenere.

mn.cue: un-TEN-able: TEN = hold, so it can’t be HELD
mn.text: The sun is melting the snow fort, and Pip and Zoe can’t hold it much longer: their position is {untenable}.

scene.alt: Two children watch their snow fort melt in the sun, unable to save it.

words.def: open to debate; also, no longer worth arguing about
words.ex: Whether to hold the picnic indoors became {moot} when the rain stopped.
words.ctx: The class argued for an hour about which bus to take on the field trip, but the question was {moot}: the trip had already been canceled because of the storm.
words.etym: From Old English mot, a meeting where people gathered to debate questions.
words.note: Moot first meant open to debate (a moot point); in American English it now often means no longer worth arguing about. Let the sentence decide. In law school, a moot court is a practice trial.

mn.cue: MOOT = MUTE: nothing left to argue
mn.text: Pip and Zoe argue over who gets the last cookie, until they see the dog already ate it. The argument goes mute: the question is {moot}.

scene.alt: Two children stop arguing over a cookie when they see the dog has already eaten it.

after.html: In logic, valid describes the shape of reasoning, not the truth of the facts. “All cats can fly; Tom is a cat; so Tom can fly” is valid (the conclusion follows) but not true, because the first premise is false. An argument that is valid and has true premises is called sound.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The theory was {untenable}: every new experiment contradicted it.

after.cap: A theory that can no longer be defended is untenable.

items.q: The team argued about which jerseys to wear to the final, but the final was canceled. The question became…
items.why: When a question no longer matters because of what happened, it is moot (the common American sense).

items.q: True or false: in its older sense, a moot point is one that is still open to debate.
items.why: True. Moot comes from an old word for a meeting where questions were debated; a moot point is debatable. In everyday American use it also means no longer relevant.

items.q: “All birds can swim. A robin is a bird. So a robin can swim.” A logician would call this reasoning…
items.why: The conclusion follows from the premises, so the reasoning is valid; but the first premise is false, so the argument is not sound.

items.q: The detective’s only clue was that both suspects liked pancakes. The connection was…
items.why: A link that rests on one tiny, slight fact is tenuous: thin and weak.
